A fixed catalogue in the companion cannot cover what Deck Apps will want (keyboard shortcuts, media keys, a Stream Deck-style grid, sensors and fan control, a T3 Code dashboard), and a generic "run this shell command" endpoint loses types and invites misuse. A plugin is a typed registry (`defineHostPlugin(id, { name: command<Payload, Result>(guard) })`) that a Deck App imports and bundles, plus an implementation the companion loads from its config. Every request names its plugin and command; the companion validates the payload with the registry's guard, and TypeScript fails a missing or mistyped implementation. The built-in `core` plugin (`capabilities`, `echo`) is always loaded, and `capabilities` lists every loaded plugin, so a Deck App can tell a computer without a plugin (`unknown_plugin`) from an offline one.

**Built-in plugins first.** The companion ships the plugins most Deck Apps need, and the SDK exports their registries, so a Deck App that uses only those needs nothing installed beyond the companion. Today that is `core` (`capabilities`, `echo`) and the read-only `systemStats`. Keys and shortcuts, media keys and opening apps or URLs are the next built-ins, and each waits for credentials (see Deferred). Plugins tied to one program, like a T3 Code dashboard, or to one machine, like fan control, stay custom.

**A custom plugin lives in its Deck App's project and ships as one file.** The author adds `hostPlugin` to `vitadeck.config.json` (`create --host-plugin` scaffolds it). `vitadeck build` bundles that implementation, with its npm dependencies and the SDK code it uses, into one ES module, the **Host Plugin File** (`<slug>.vdplugin`), written next to the `.vdapp.zip`. The user runs `vitadeck-host-companion install <file>`, which copies it to `~/.vitadeck/plugins/`, and a running companion reloads that directory and every `--plugin` file when they change, so `vitadeck dev` plus `start --plugin` is the author's edit loop. The file is plain JavaScript rather than a zip like the **Deck App Package**, because it has nothing to carry besides code; the companion imports a copy named by its content hash with an `.mjs` extension, since Node imports no unknown extension and bundled CommonJS needs a file URL for `createRequire`, and a rebuild gets a new name instead of a cached module. The companion checks the default export's shape (`id`, a `Map` of commands) and a `HostCommandError`'s name and code rather than classes, since each file bundles its own copy of the SDK. That shape is the contract between a file built with one SDK version and a companion of another.

Considered for custom plugins: npm packages the companion resolves by name (rejected: an author would publish a package per Deck App, and a global companion cannot resolve packages installed elsewhere); a zip with a manifest (rejected until a plugin needs files besides code); and serving the implementation from the Vita at link time (rejected: the Vita would push code that the computer runs).

**Two CLIs, one per machine role.** `@vitadeck/sdk`'s `vitadeck` builds Deck Apps and Host Plugin Files; `@vitadeck/host-companion`'s `vitadeck-host-companion` runs on any computer a Vita controls. A single `vitadeck host ...` would make every user install the Deck App build toolchain (Babel, rolldown) to run a server. A second bin in the SDK would also break `npx @vitadeck/sdk`, which works only while the package has exactly one bin. The companion bundles the SDK code it needs and has no dependencies.

## Use
```sh
pnpm --dir js host-companion start
vitadeck-host-companion start

Serves `POST /command` on every interface, port 8797. The port never moves to a free one, because the Vita stores the URL; if it is busy, `start` exits with an error. It prints its URLs, the loaded plugins, and one line per request (time, peer, `plugin.command`, result, duration). Payloads are never logged.
```sh
pnpm --dir js host-companion link 192.168.1.177
vitadeck-host-companion link 192.168.1.177

Open Host Control in the VitaDeck Shell and pass the address it shows (add `:port` if it is not 8798). `link` checks that `start` is answering, then tells VitaDeck where to send commands. One Vita can link several computers, and one computer can link several Vitas.

Options: `--port N` (both commands; use the same one for `link` if you started with it), `--plugin <specifier>` (repeatable, `start` only, in addition to the config), `--advertise <ip>` (`link` only), `--config <path>`.

## Plugins
Every companion has the built-in plugins: `core` (`capabilities`, `echo`) and `systemStats` (`read`: CPU, memory, uptime). A Deck App imports their registries from `@vitadeck/sdk/host-control`.
A Deck App that needs more brings its own plugin as a **Host Plugin File** (`.vdplugin`), which its author ships next to the `.vdapp.zip`:
```sh
vitadeck-host-companion install lights.vdplugin
vitadeck-host-companion remove lights

`install` copies the file to `~/.vitadeck/plugins/`, named by the plugin's id, and a running companion loads it at once. A plugin runs with your permissions on this computer, so install only plugins you trust.

To write one, scaffold a Deck App with `npx @vitadeck/sdk create my-app --host-plugin`; the [SDK README](../sdk/README.md#host-control) explains the files. While you work on it, `start --plugin ./dist` loads your build, takes precedence over an installed copy, and reloads every time `vitadeck build` or `vitadeck dev` writes it. A broken build keeps the previous version running.

export const lightsPlugin = defineHostPlugin("lights", {
toggle: command<{ room: string }, { on: boolean }>(isRoom),

- `./companion`: the implementation, which default-exports `implementHostPlugin(registry, implementations)` from `@vitadeck/host-companion`. A missing or mistyped implementation fails `tsc`.
